variants.title: Run the filtering pipeline
variants.context: A source snapshot becomes a reviewable release in five stages: freeze the snapshot, apply deterministic gates, apply model-backed gates, audit slices and uncertainty, then publish an immutable release. Raw inputs stay immutable and every stage emits a disposition, a reason code, and component versions.
variants.prompt: A new source snapshot arrives and the team wants a signed dataset release from it. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Publish an immutable release binding retained shards to the policy, code, models, reason counts, and slice evidence.
Apply deterministic gates that reject unreadable encodings, invalid schemas, missing metadata, and exact duplicates.
Freeze the source snapshot with its URI, retrieval time, usage basis, content hash, and parser version.
Audit slices and uncertainty by sampling accepted and rejected records and routing ambiguous cases to reviewers.
Apply model-backed gates that score language, relevance, quality, safety, and privacy with versioned models.

variants.hint: Which stage is cheap enough and certain enough to run before any model is loaded?
variants.explanation: Deterministic contract gates run before learned gates so expensive scoring never touches records that already failed a testable rule.

variants.title: Run the filtering pipeline
variants.context: A source snapshot becomes a reviewable release in five stages: freeze the snapshot, apply deterministic gates, apply model-backed gates, audit slices and uncertainty, then publish an immutable release. Raw inputs stay immutable and every stage emits a disposition, a reason code, and component versions.
variants.prompt: A record with a valid schema but an unreadable character encoding enters the pipeline. Put the stages it touches in order, ending where it stops.

items.text: The quarantined record is counted in the disposition reconciliation and kept access controlled.
A deterministic gate fails the record because the encoding cannot be decoded.
The snapshot holding the record is frozen with its content hash and parser version.
The record is quarantined with a first-failure reason code and skips every later gate.

variants.hint: An early-exit cascade stops spending compute the moment a record fails.
variants.explanation: A failed record still needs a reason code and a counted disposition, because quarantine is a recorded decision rather than a silent drop.

variants.title: Run the filtering pipeline
variants.context: A source snapshot becomes a reviewable release in five stages: freeze the snapshot, apply deterministic gates, apply model-backed gates, audit slices and uncertainty, then publish an immutable release. Raw inputs stay immutable and every stage emits a disposition, a reason code, and component versions.
variants.prompt: A threshold is being raised, so the release is reprocessed under a new policy version. Put the work in order.

items.text: Reprocess the immutable source snapshot and reconcile counts across every disposition.
Sample accepted, rejected, and uncertain records and report both error directions by slice.
Sign the release by binding shard hashes, policy identity, reason counts, audit results, and known limits.
Freeze the eligibility rules, thresholds, and model and parser hashes as a new policy version.

variants.hint: The snapshot does not change during a policy change; something else must.
variants.explanation: Reprocessing under a new policy version is what makes a threshold change auditable, because the same immutable snapshot yields a comparable before-and-after.

variants.title: Audit a threshold
variants.context: A threshold audit compares automated dispositions against human-reviewed eligibility labels. False rejection divides rejected eligible records by all eligible records, leakage divides accepted ineligible records by all accepted records, and the release passes only when both declared guardrails hold.
variants.prompt: A quality threshold is proposed for one reviewed slice. Put the audit steps in order.

items.text: Compute leakage by dividing accepted ineligible records by all accepted records.
Predict eligible for every record scoring at or above the threshold.
Compare each automated decision against the human-reviewed eligibility label.
Pass the slice only when both declared guardrails hold.
Compute false rejection by dividing rejected eligible records by all eligible records.

variants.hint: The two rates use different denominators, so they cannot be computed in the same pass over one bucket.
variants.explanation: False rejection measures coverage lost and leakage measures risk published, so both are computed and both guardrails must hold before a slice passes.

variants.title: Audit a threshold
variants.context: A threshold audit compares automated dispositions against human-reviewed eligibility labels. False rejection divides rejected eligible records by all eligible records, leakage divides accepted ineligible records by all accepted records, and the release passes only when both declared guardrails hold.
variants.prompt: A slice clears the leakage guardrail but fails the false-rejection guardrail. Put the response in order.

items.text: Identify which gate produced the rejections and whether its threshold or its features caused them.
Sample the rejected records that reviewers marked eligible and read the reason codes.
Report the failing rate together with its counts so reviewers can see how stable the percentage is.
Propose a policy version change and record the before-and-after evidence for review.

variants.hint: Start with what the failing number is made of before changing anything.
variants.explanation: A rate without its counts can be an artifact of a small sample, so the audit reads the actual rejected records before a threshold is moved.

variants.title: Audit a threshold
variants.context: A threshold audit compares automated dispositions against human-reviewed eligibility labels. False rejection divides rejected eligible records by all eligible records, leakage divides accepted ineligible records by all accepted records, and the release passes only when both declared guardrails hold.
variants.prompt: A record scores just below the threshold and reviewers disagree about its eligibility. Put the handling in order.

items.text: Include the disagreement and adjudication in the release evidence for the slice.
Mark the record uncertain because the available evidence cannot settle the disposition automatically.
Record the reviewer disagreement and the adjudicated outcome rather than treating one label as ground truth.
Route the record to human review under the written reviewer guidance.

variants.hint: Uncertainty is a disposition of its own, not a rounding decision.
variants.explanation: Preserving an uncertainty path keeps borderline records out of both published and rejected sets until a reviewed decision exists.

variants.title: Compute cascade CPU
variants.context: An early-exit cascade quarantines a failed record with its first-failure reason and skips the later gates. Stage CPU is the records evaluated at that stage times the measured milliseconds per record, and total CPU is the sum across the cascade.
variants.prompt: A cascade takes 10,000 records. The schema gate costs 0.2 ms per record and rejects 3,000. The dedup gate costs 1.5 ms per record and rejects 1,000 of the survivors. The classifier gate costs 4 ms per record. What is the total fixture CPU in milliseconds?
variants.hint: Each gate only pays for the records that actually reach it.
variants.explanation: Total CPU sums records evaluated times cost per record at each stage, and early exit is what keeps the expensive gate off already-failed records.

mistakes.feedback: Every gate was charged all 10,000 records; early exit means later gates never see the rejected ones.
Only the classifier stage was counted; the two cheaper stages still consume CPU.

variants.title: Compute cascade CPU
variants.context: An early-exit cascade quarantines a failed record with its first-failure reason and skips the later gates. Stage CPU is the records evaluated at that stage times the measured milliseconds per record, and total CPU is the sum across the cascade.
variants.prompt: The same 10,000 records are run with the classifier first. The classifier costs 4 ms per record and rejects 4,000. The schema gate then costs 0.2 ms per record and rejects 1,000 of the survivors. The dedup gate costs 1.5 ms per record. What is the total fixture CPU in milliseconds?
variants.hint: Reordering does not change the per-record costs, only how many records each gate sees.
variants.explanation: Gate order changes compute and first-failure reason counts, which is why putting the expensive gate first costs more even when the retained set is identical.

mistakes.feedback: That is the cost of the cheap-gate-first order; this cascade charges the 4 ms gate all 10,000 records.
The 0.2 ms schema stage was left out of the sum.

variants.title: Compute cascade CPU
variants.context: An early-exit cascade quarantines a failed record with its first-failure reason and skips the later gates. Stage CPU is the records evaluated at that stage times the measured milliseconds per record, and total CPU is the sum across the cascade.
variants.prompt: A run reports 40,000 records evaluated at the schema gate at 0.05 ms each, 26,000 at the dedup gate at 0.9 ms each, and 9,000 at the classifier gate at 6 ms each. What is the total CPU in milliseconds?
variants.hint: The evaluated counts are already given, so no funnel needs to be reconstructed.
variants.explanation: Stage CPU is evaluated records times measured milliseconds per record, and the total is the sum of those stage costs.

mistakes.feedback: All 40,000 records were charged to every gate instead of the evaluated counts reported per stage.
The schema stage was omitted from the sum.

variants.title: Assign the gate family
variants.context: Filtering uses four gate families with different jobs: contract gates check decoding, schema, and source eligibility; redundancy gates remove exact or near duplicates under a declared cluster policy; learned gates make bounded decisions from calibrated model scores; human review handles uncertainty and disagreement.
variants.prompt: A filtering policy is being written. Match each gate family to the job it owns.

pairs.label: Contract gates
pairs.detail: Check decoding, schema, length bounds, required metadata, and source eligibility with reproducible rules.

pairs.label: Redundancy gates
pairs.detail: Remove exact or near duplicates under a declared unit, normalization, similarity method, and cluster policy.

pairs.label: Learned gates
pairs.detail: Make bounded decisions from calibrated model scores, with thresholds and model versions treated as release inputs.

pairs.label: Human review
pairs.detail: Handle ambiguous and high-impact cases under written guidance, tracking disagreement and adjudication.

variants.hint: Ask which family could be replayed from the same bytes alone.
variants.explanation: The families differ in what they need to reach a decision, which is why they are versioned and audited separately rather than averaged together.

variants.title: Assign the gate family
variants.context: Filtering uses four gate families with different jobs: contract gates check decoding, schema, and source eligibility; redundancy gates remove exact or near duplicates under a declared cluster policy; learned gates make bounded decisions from calibrated model scores; human review handles uncertainty and disagreement.
variants.prompt: Four records fail in different ways. Match each record to the gate family that owns its disposition.

pairs.label: A payload whose encoding cannot be decoded and whose required metadata is missing
A byte-identical copy of a page already retained under a different URL
A page whose relevance to the target domain has to be scored by a versioned model
A borderline record where the available evidence cannot settle the disposition

variants.hint: Two of these can be decided from the bytes alone; the other two cannot.
variants.explanation: Routing each failure to the family that owns it is what makes reason codes meaningful when the release is audited.

variants.title: Assign the gate family
variants.context: Filtering uses four gate families with different jobs: contract gates check decoding, schema, and source eligibility; redundancy gates remove exact or near duplicates under a declared cluster policy; learned gates make bounded decisions from calibrated model scores; human review handles uncertainty and disagreement.
variants.prompt: A second batch raises four more cases. Match each case to the gate family that owns it.

pairs.label: A source whose usage basis is not on the allowed list in the release contract
Forty near-identical listings from one template that need a declared cluster policy
A passage whose safety disposition depends on a calibrated threshold and model version
A high-impact case where two reviewers disagree and adjudication must be recorded

variants.hint: Source eligibility is a contract question even though it sounds like a judgment call.
variants.explanation: Eligibility rules stated in the contract stay deterministic, while anything needing a calibrated score or a judgment moves to a learned gate or a reviewer.

variants.title: Bound what a score can settle
variants.context: An automated score is evidence about a policy decision, not a measurement of truth. Independent requirements must not be collapsed into one weighted average, a strong dimension must not cancel a hard exclusion, and there has to be an uncertainty path instead of forcing every record into keep or delete.
variants.prompt: A record scores 0.94 on language quality but a privacy detector leaves an unresolved sensitive-data flag, and policy says unresolved sensitive data blocks release. What is the right disposition?
options: Publish it, since the quality score is far above the release threshold.
Hold it as uncertain, since a strong dimension cannot cancel a hard exclusion.
Lower the privacy threshold so the flag resolves and the record can publish.
optionFeedback: A high score on one dimension is evidence about quality, not about the privacy policy the record is failing.
Hard exclusions block release regardless of other scores, and an unresolved flag belongs on the uncertainty path.
Moving a threshold to make a specific record pass changes the policy for the whole release without any audit evidence.
variants.hint: Ask whether these two signals are answering the same question.
variants.explanation: Independent requirements stay independent, so a strong quality score never cancels a license, privacy, or safety exclusion.

variants.title: Bound what a score can settle
variants.context: An automated score is evidence about a policy decision, not a measurement of truth. Independent requirements must not be collapsed into one weighted average, a strong dimension must not cancel a hard exclusion, and there has to be an uncertainty path instead of forcing every record into keep or delete.
variants.prompt: To simplify monitoring, a team proposes one weighted score combining license, privacy, quality, and safety signals, publishing anything above 0.8. What should the reviewer say?
options: Approve it with a higher cutoff of 0.9 so weak dimensions matter less.
Approve it, because one number is easier to alert on and to explain.
Reject it, because averaging lets one strong signal outvote a hard exclusion.
optionFeedback: Raising the cutoff changes how often the average is outvoted but never removes the possibility.
Ease of monitoring is not a reason to make a license failure cancelable by a quality score.
Collapsing independent requirements into an average is exactly what lets a hard exclusion be outvoted.
variants.hint: Ask what the average allows that the separate rules forbid.
variants.explanation: A single quality score cannot explain a decision, which is why dispositions carry policy version, gate versions, and reason codes instead.

variants.title: Bound what a score can settle
variants.context: An automated score is evidence about a policy decision, not a measurement of truth. Independent requirements must not be collapsed into one weighted average, a strong dimension must not cancel a hard exclusion, and there has to be an uncertainty path instead of forcing every record into keep or delete.
variants.prompt: A safety classifier flags a clinical training passage that quotes abusive language in order to describe it. Policy distinguishes quoted and clinical context from targeted abuse. What should happen?
options: Lower the safety threshold globally so clinical passages stop being flagged.
Reject the passage, since the safety classifier fired on it.
Route it to a reviewer, since the policy turns on context the score cannot see.
optionFeedback: A global threshold change trades this false positive for leakage everywhere else in the release.
Acting on the classifier alone applies a policy the classifier was never able to evaluate.
Reviewer escalation is the designed path when policy depends on quoted, counterspeech, educational, or clinical context.
variants.hint: Ask whether the classifier is measuring the thing the policy actually prohibits.
variants.explanation: Safety policy names a prohibited behavior in context, so a context-blind score routes ambiguous cases to review rather than deciding them.
